prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN) -- More than 100 Romanians fled their homes Tuesday night in Belfast, Northern Ireland, following what politicians called "racist attacks and intimidation." A Romanian woman and her child are escorted by police in Belfast on Wednesday. "On Tuesday evening, when the Romanians saw their windows starting to be smashed, they felt the threats were very real and contacted the police," said Trish Morgan, the media relations manager at the Belfast City Church, which took them in. A church member was advised by the police that "the situation was getting too tense," and that the group -- 113 people in all -- needed to find a safe place that could accommodate them quickly. The member contacted the church, and that's where they went, Morgan said. The Romanians were "quite scared" upon arrival at the church but "relieved to be out of the situation," she added. British Prime Minister Gordon Brown Wednesday condemned what one member of Parliament called "appalling racist attacks," and said he hoped the authorities would be able to "take all the action necessary to protect them." Martin McGuinness, the deputy first minister of Northern Ireland -- a province of the United Kingdom -- visited the families on Wednesday, his party Sinn Fein announced. "People are shocked and completely disgusted by this incident," he said in a statement "I came here this morning to show very clearly my commitment to facing up to any form of intimidation in our community, no matter where it may come from. "I met with numerous families who are genuinely fearful for their lives and those of their families; I held a five-day-old baby girl in my arms today. She was born in Belfast and now forced to leave her home as a result of attacks by racist, criminal thugs," McGuinness said. He was speaking at the O-Zone leisure center, where the families have moved because the space is larger than the church. Race-hate crime in south Belfast has increased in the past six months, Sinn Fein equality and human rights expert Vincent Parker said. The incident came only a day after violence broke out at an anti-racism rally in support of Romanians in Belfast. Belfast Lord Mayor Naomi Long called Monday's scuffles "totally unacceptable." "A small minority of people have sadly taken away from an event which had been organized by the local community to show solidarity for their Romanian neighbors, and to express their abhorrence at their homes being subjected to racist attacks," she said Tuesday. CNN's Eve Bower contributed to this report.

LONDON, England (CNN) — Over 100 Romanian residents left their Belfast homes on Tuesday night after incidents that politicians described as racist violence and harassment.

On Wednesday, police accompanied a Romanian mother and her child in Belfast.

Trish Morgan, media relations manager for Belfast City Church, which provided refuge to the group, said the Romanians contacted police on Tuesday evening after their windows began to be broken and they realized the danger was serious.

According to Morgan, police told a church member that tensions were escalating and that all 113 people needed to be moved quickly to a secure location large enough to hold them. The member then approached Belfast City Church, and the group went there.

Morgan said they arrived frightened but were also grateful to have escaped the threatening circumstances.

On Wednesday, British Prime Minister Gordon Brown denounced the incidents, which a member of Parliament characterized as horrific racist assaults. Brown expressed hope that officials would take every necessary measure to ensure the Romanians’ safety.

Martin McGuinness, Northern Ireland’s deputy first minister, visited the displaced families Wednesday, according to his party, Sinn Fein. Northern Ireland is part of the United Kingdom.

In a statement, McGuinness said the public was horrified and deeply repulsed by what had happened. He explained that his morning visit was intended to demonstrate his determination to confront intimidation in the community, regardless of its source.

McGuinness said he had spoken with many families who sincerely feared for their own lives and those of their relatives. He also described holding a five-day-old girl who had been born in Belfast but was already being driven from her home because of attacks by racist criminals.

He made the remarks at the O-Zone leisure center, where the families had relocated because it offered more room than the church.

Vincent Parker, Sinn Fein’s specialist on equality and human rights, said racially motivated crime in south Belfast had risen during the previous six months.

The episode occurred just one day after clashes erupted at a Belfast anti-racism demonstration organized to support the Romanian community.

Belfast Lord Mayor Naomi Long described Monday’s disorder as entirely intolerable. In comments made Tuesday, she said a small group had unfortunately undermined an event arranged by local residents to stand with their Romanian neighbors and condemn the racist targeting of their homes.

CNN’s Eve Bower contributed to the report.

### More than 100 Romanians flee Belfast homes after racist attacks

**BELFAST, Northern Ireland** — More than 100 Romanian residents, including families with young children, have fled their homes in south Belfast following a series of racist attacks and threats, police and community representatives said.

The residents left after homes were vandalized, windows were smashed and families were subjected to intimidation and racist abuse. Many sought temporary shelter at a local church before being moved to emergency accommodation.

Most of those displaced are members of the Roma community who had settled in the area in search of work and a safer life.

Northern Ireland’s political leaders condemned the attacks, describing them as shameful and unrepresentative of Belfast. Police said they were investigating the violence and increasing patrols in affected neighborhoods.

Community volunteers provided food, bedding and other necessities to the families, some of whom said they were considering leaving Northern Ireland altogether because they no longer felt safe.

Anti-racism campaigners warned that the intimidation appeared coordinated and called for stronger protection for migrant communities.

Authorities said efforts were underway to find secure temporary housing for the displaced residents while the investigation continued.

In mid-June 2009, about 115 Romanian Roma—roughly 20 families, including many children—were forced from their homes in the Lisburn Road area of south Belfast after several nights of racist intimidation. Attackers shouted abuse, issued threats, damaged houses and broke windows. The families first took refuge in a local church, were moved to emergency accommodation, and were then placed at a secure location. Most subsequently chose to return to Romania, despite offers of help to remain.

The attacks drew widespread condemnation:

- **Prime Minister Gordon Brown** called the violence and intimidation “completely unacceptable,” said the families had a right to live safely in Northern Ireland, and urged that those responsible be brought to justice.
- **Deputy First Minister Martin McGuinness** described the attacks as shameful and disgraceful, stressing that the perpetrators were a small minority who did not represent Belfast or Northern Ireland. He said the Romanian families should be supported and made to feel welcome.
- **Belfast Lord Mayor Naomi Long** condemned the intimidation as a deeply damaging display of racism. She emphasized that the attackers did not speak for the wider community, called for a strong police and community response, and expressed dismay that people who had come to Belfast to work and build lives had been driven from their homes.

The episode became one of Northern Ireland’s most prominent hate-crime incidents and prompted renewed debate about policing, community leadership and protection for migrant and Roma communities.

More than 100 Romanian immigrants, including many children, were forced from their homes in south Belfast in June 2009 after sustained racist intimidation. Families reported verbal abuse, threats, attacks on houses and broken windows. They initially took shelter in Belfast City Church before being moved to emergency accommodation.

Church spokesperson Trish Morgan described the families as deeply frightened: **“They are very scared. They have been intimidated and attacked in their own homes, and they do not feel safe going back.”** Church members and volunteers provided food, bedding and other assistance while the authorities arranged temporary housing.

Northern Ireland’s political leaders condemned the violence. First Minister Peter Robinson called the attacks **“a disgrace to Northern Ireland”** and said those responsible did not represent the wider community. Deputy First Minister Martin McGuinness described the intimidation as **“totally and absolutely appalling,”** insisting that racism had no place in society.

Local representatives likewise denounced the perpetrators. South Belfast MP Alasdair McDonnell said the attacks were the work of a small racist minority and urged residents to stand with the Romanian families. Belfast Lord Mayor Naomi Long said the city should be known for welcoming newcomers, not for driving them from their homes.

Police treated the incidents as racially motivated hate crimes. Community organisations warned that the intimidation exposed a broader problem of racism against migrant workers in Northern Ireland and called for stronger protection, enforcement and long-term support for affected families.
